**Abstract.** Education systems count disadvantaged students who achieve highly as a success. We ask how these resilient students rate their own lives. With PISA 2025 data for `r N_mx$systems` education systems, we divide students by national quarters of family background and reading achievement and compare resilient students with the other groups in the same school. Resilient students have the lowest life satisfaction of the 16 groups. With sex, age and grade held fixed, they are `r mea("S1A4","M3")` SD below advantaged top achievers and `r mea("R-AL","M3")` SD below advantaged low achievers, but only `r mea("R-PL","M3")` SD below disadvantaged low achievers. The gap to advantaged top achievers is similar across systems and spans the whole answer scale; response styles do not produce it. A weaker sense of belonging and less family support account for about a third of it. Against disadvantaged low achievers the same relationships hide part of the gap, which doubles once they are held fixed. Indicators of academic resilience should be reported with students' own evaluations of their lives and compared with advantaged students.

**Keywords:** academic resilience; life satisfaction; subjective wellbeing; socio-emotional skills; PISA; response scales

# Introduction

Education systems are judged in part by their resilient students, the children of the poorest families who score among the best in their country. The OECD reports the share of such students for every system that takes part in PISA [@oecd2026vol1], and a body of research asks what schools and countries do to raise it [@agasisti2018]. The indicator records a test score. How these students evaluate their own lives, an outcome that child-indicator research treats as important in its own right [@benarieh2008], is not part of it.

In PISA 2025 they evaluate their lives less favourably than any other group. When students are divided by the national quarters of family background and of reading achievement, resilient students have the lowest mean life satisfaction of the 16 groups, `r f2(mat("mean","S1A4"))` on a scale from 0 to 10, against `r f2(mat("mean","S4A4"))` for advantaged top achievers and `r f2(mat("mean","S4A1"))` for advantaged low achievers. Among advantaged students life satisfaction barely depends on achievement. Among disadvantaged students it falls as achievement rises.

This paper estimates how much less satisfied resilient students are than advantaged top achievers, advantaged low achievers and disadvantaged low achievers in the same school, in the `r N_mx$systems` education systems of PISA 2025 that allow the comparison. All groups enter one model, with advantaged top achievers as the reference. With sex, age and grade held fixed, resilient students report life satisfaction `r mea("S1A4","M3")` SD (SE `r mse("S1A4","M3")`), or `r mea("S1A4","M3",2,"pt")` points, below advantaged top achievers and `r mea("R-AL","M3")` SD below advantaged low achievers. The gap to advantaged top achievers is negative in `r mneg("S1A4","M3")` of `r mn("S1A4","M3")` systems and close to the same everywhere; the variation between systems is about what sampling error produces. Against disadvantaged low achievers the gap is smaller, `r mea("R-PL","M3")` SD. In no system are resilient students significantly more satisfied than any of the three groups.

Against advantaged top achievers the whole distribution of answers shifts down. Resilient students are `r appa("thr:M3:ge8:R-AT")` percentage points less likely to answer 8 or more and `r app("thr:M3:le3:R-AT")` points more likely to answer 3 or less. Response styles, fast answering and the use of numerical scales in general do not account for the gap.

Relationships account for much of the gap to advantaged students of the same achievement. Holding skills, mindsets and relationships fixed halves it, to `r mea("S1A4","M5")` SD, and a decomposition that does not depend on the order of the controls attributes `r gla("R-AT","REL")` SD to relationships, mainly to a weaker sense of belonging at school and less family support. These characteristics do not account for the gap to advantaged low achievers, and against disadvantaged low achievers they work the other way: resilient students have more of them, and holding them fixed widens that gap to `r mea("R-PL","M5")` SD. Lower life satisfaction among high achievers appears in both status groups, but the difference between top and other achievers is larger among disadvantaged students, by `r mea("DiD2","M3")` SD. A causal forest finds no variation in the gap within schools; in linear models it is smaller for students with a stronger sense of belonging.

The direction of the raw difference has been reported before. In its report on PISA 2018 the OECD notes that, on average across OECD countries, a smaller share of resilient than of other disadvantaged students are satisfied with life [@oecd2019]. That comparison cuts the scale at 7, takes all other disadvantaged students as the reference group, uses no controls and gives no magnitude in the text. The sign reverses in several countries, and the chapter reads the evidence as mildly favourable to resilient students. A second line of work finds an inverted-U relation between life satisfaction and achievement in PISA 2018, with the most satisfied students scoring below the moderately satisfied [@oecd2019b; @li2024]. @siebecke2026 finds the same curve among resilient students in Sweden, relating wellbeing to achievement inside the resilient group. The third relevant literature comes from health research in the United States. Disadvantaged young people who succeed report good psychological adjustment in these studies and carry physiological costs, a pattern known as skin-deep resilience [@brody2013; @miller2015; @chen2022b]. None of these studies measures life satisfaction.

We add three things to this work. The first is the reference group. The OECD's comparison with other disadvantaged students is the one on which the existing evidence rests, and it gives the smallest gap. Set against advantaged students, of the same or of lower achievement, resilient students are clearly and consistently less satisfied, in `r msig("S1A4","M3")` systems significantly. The second is an account of the gap. Relationships at school and at home account for a large part of the distance to advantaged top achievers and none of the distance to advantaged low achievers, and they hide part of the distance to other disadvantaged students. The third concerns measurement. We locate the gap on the scale and test whether it is a matter of reporting, which bears on any child indicator built on the share of students above a cut point.

We use "cost" for a difference between groups of students. The design compares students within schools and does not identify what resilient students would report had they achieved less or come from richer families. @clarke2020 warns against reading differences of this kind as a trade-off between wellbeing and achievement, and on average the two are positively related [@bucker2018; @kaya2021]. Our claim is that disadvantaged students who achieve highly rate their lives lower than the students they are compared with, and that the gap to advantaged students is the larger one.

Section 2 sets out the evidence behind four research questions. Section 3 describes the data and the 16 groups, and Section 4 the nested models and the threats to them. Section 5 reports the comparisons, where on the scale the gap lies, what accounts for it, whether it is specific to disadvantaged students, where it differs, and the robustness checks. Section 6 discusses what the results mean for academic resilience as an indicator, and Section 7 concludes.

# Background and research questions

Research on academic resilience asks which students, schools and systems produce high achievement against the odds [@agasisti2018]. How the students who achieve it evaluate their lives is a separate question. Four bodies of evidence bear on it, and each leaves one question open.
<!-- The search protocol, logs and evidence table behind this section are in literature/ (scoping_review.md, evidence_table.md, review_structure.md). -->

## Achievement and life satisfaction

On average, students who achieve more are slightly more satisfied with their lives. Two meta-analyses find a small positive correlation between achievement and subjective wellbeing, about 0.16 in the first [@bucker2018; @kaya2021]. A systematic review in *Child Indicators Research* calls the evidence inconsistent [@amholt2020].

The relation is not linear. In PISA 2018, students who answer 9 or 10 score 16 points lower in reading than other students once their socio-economic profile is accounted for, and those who answer 7 or 8 score 15 points higher [@oecd2019b]. The same inverted U appears in mainland China and in Sweden [@li2024; @siebecke2026]. If it holds among disadvantaged students, their high achievers should give fewer of the highest answers.

For disadvantaged students who achieve, the best-developed evidence points the other way. In the studies of skin-deep resilience, young people from poor families who show high competence or self-control have fewer depressive symptoms than their peers, and the cost appears in physical health [@brody2013; @miller2015; @chen2022b]. These studies do not measure life satisfaction, and their physical cost appears mostly in Black and Latinx samples in the United States [@brody2016; @prag2019].

The closest antecedent is the OECD's chapter on resilience and wellbeing in PISA 2018 [@oecd2019]. It compares resilient students with all other disadvantaged students on the share answering 7 or more, without controls. A smaller share of resilient students is satisfied on average across OECD countries and in three systems, and a larger share in three others. The chapter gives no magnitude. A comparison within schools that sets resilient students against groups that differ from them in background, in achievement or in both is missing, and the evidence above predicts different signs for it.

> **RQ1.** How does the life satisfaction of resilient students compare with that of advantaged top achievers, advantaged low achievers and disadvantaged low achievers in the same school, and at which answers does the difference lie?

## What resilient students bring

Resilient students differ from other disadvantaged students in more than test scores. They report more self-efficacy, more motivation to master tasks and a stronger sense of belonging at school [@oecd2019]. In the OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills, high achievers have more of the skills of task performance and open-mindedness, among them persistence and curiosity [@oecd2024]. A growth mindset, the belief that intelligence can be developed, also goes with achievement among poor students: in Chile, students from the poorest families who hold it score as high as much richer students who do not [@claro2016].

The same characteristics are associated with higher life satisfaction. In the OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills every skill measured is positively related to it [@oecd2021; @oecd2024]. Among relationships, family support is the strongest correlate of adolescents' life satisfaction across 42 countries and regions [@bi2021], and belonging and freedom from bullying are consistent correlates in PISA and in the Children's Worlds survey [@oecd2019b; @savahl2019].

These two facts imply suppression. If resilient students have more of what raises life satisfaction, a raw comparison with low achievers nets whatever high achievement takes from life satisfaction against what skills and relationships add, and it understates the first. Against advantaged students who achieve as highly, the balance may run the other way, because support at home and at school also differs by family background. We found no study that holds socio-emotional skills fixed when it compares the wellbeing of high and low achievers, so the size of either effect is unknown.

One qualification limits what PISA 2025 can show. The skills most related to school grades are curiosity, persistence and self-control, and the skills most related to life satisfaction are optimism, trust and emotional regulation [@guo2023; @oecd2021]. PISA 2025 measures six skills of the first kind, so the masking we can estimate is masking by task-oriented skills.

> **RQ2.** How much of these differences do socio-emotional skills, mindsets and relationships account for, and which of them?

## Disadvantage among achievers

Lower life satisfaction among high achievers could be general, or it could belong to those who achieve from a poor background. The literature is divided, and most of it concerns adults who have completed a move between social classes.

A larger penalty for disadvantaged achievers has some support. Among German high-school students, achievement is related to life satisfaction only where the mother has at least the education the student is pursuing [@crede2015]. In panel data, upward mobility lowers life satisfaction in the United Kingdom and has no effect in Switzerland [@hadjar2015].

Most quantitative studies find no such penalty. People who move far up fare better on subjective wellbeing than those who stay in the working class in Britain [@chan2018], and in 44 European countries the life satisfaction of the mobile reflects their classes of origin and destination, with nothing added by mobility itself [@dhoore2019]. The cost of achievement pressure has been documented mainly among the affluent, in high-achieving schools [@luthar2020]. @breen2024 argue that a mobility effect is not identified as such and that researchers can instead estimate how the effect of a destination differs by origin. We adopt that form, with high achievement as the destination and family background as the origin.

A second comparison sets disadvantaged achievers against advantaged ones. In the United Kingdom, children from low-income families who were in the top quarter of ability at age 5 are about 0.3 SD less happy at 14 than equally able children from high-income families [@jerrim2025], and competent inner-city adolescents in the United States are more depressed and anxious than competent adolescents from low-stress backgrounds [@luthar1991]. This comparison holds achievement fixed and lets background differ. It includes the general association of family background with life satisfaction, and it shows how far resilient students are from the group that is best placed on both counts.

> **RQ3.** Is the lower life satisfaction of high achievers specific to disadvantaged students?

## Where the gap may differ

Two mechanisms could make the gap depend on where a resilient student goes to school. The first is comparison with schoolmates. School-average achievement lowers academic self-concept in a 26-country study of 15-year-olds [@marsh2003], and in German panel data high performers in higher-performing classes report lower life satisfaction than high performers elsewhere [@rathmann2018]. The second is status mismatch. Low-income students in the United States show more psychosocial problems as the share of better-off schoolmates rises [@crosnoe2009].

The evidence against is at least as strong. A scoping review finds that low socio-economic position harms wellbeing more in poorer schools [@herke2022], and schools account for only 5 to 9 per cent of the variance in wellbeing indicators in PISA 2015 [@govorova2020].

Sex, aspirations and skills are the remaining candidates. Girls report lower life satisfaction than boys in all 33 countries of one PISA 2015 analysis [@marquez2024]. Unmet educational expectations bring almost no long-term emotional cost once attainment is taken into account [@reynolds2010]. Among skills, self-control predicts fewer depressive symptoms among disadvantaged young people [@miller2015], and for curiosity the literature gives no prediction in either direction. A growth mindset raises the achievement of lower-achieving students in a national experiment in the United States [@yeager2019]. Resilient students also report more self-efficacy and a stronger sense of belonging than other disadvantaged students [@oecd2019]. Whether any of these beliefs and attitudes changes how high achievers evaluate their lives has not been tested. Skills rated by the student call for caution, because self-ratings share reporting habits with the outcome [@guo2023; @lira2022].

We found no study that tests any of these characteristics as a moderator of the relation between achievement and life satisfaction among adolescents. With fourteen candidates and no ranking among them, we examine them jointly.

> **RQ4.** Does the gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers vary with the school context, sex, aspirations, mindsets or socio-emotional skills of resilient students?

# Data

## Data and sample

We use the public student files of PISA 2025, the OECD's assessment of 15-year-olds enrolled in school [@oecd2026data]. `r N$systems` education systems fielded the life-satisfaction item and at least four of the six socio-emotional skill scales, and they contribute `r big(N$students)` students. Models that compare students within schools need a school identifier in the public file and at least 80 students in each of the four groups we compare (defined below). `r N_mx$systems` systems meet both conditions. In them, `r big(N_mx$students)` of `r big(N_mx$all)` students are observed on every variable of the models, among them about `r big(N_mx$R)` resilient students, `r big(N_mx$PL)` disadvantaged low achievers, `r big(N_mx$AL)` advantaged low achievers and `r big(N_mx$AT)` advantaged top achievers. @tbl-systems gives the mean of every variable by system, and @tbl-avail the share of students observed on each.

## Measures

*Life satisfaction.* Students answer the question "Overall, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?" on a scale from 0 to 10. We analyse the item standardised within each system, where one SD is about 2.3 scale points, and the share of students giving each answer.

*Family background and achievement.* Family background is the PISA index of economic, social and cultural status. Achievement is the reading score, computed separately for each of the ten plausible values. As a check we repeat the main estimates with the science score.

*Socio-emotional skills.* PISA 2025 contains six self-rated scales: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem-solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting and self-regulated learning. They enter the models separately. In 17 systems a parent also rates the student's self-regulation.

*Growth mindset.* Students say how far they agree that "you have a certain amount of intelligence, and you really can't do much to change it". Those who disagree or strongly disagree are coded as holding a growth mindset. The item was not fielded in Spain.

*Science self-efficacy and enjoyment of science.* Two scales from the science questionnaire, the major domain of PISA 2025. We use them as indicators of academic self-efficacy and enjoyment of learning; achievement in reading and science is highly correlated. Both are standardised within system.

*Relationships.* We use four scales: sense of belonging at school, exposure to bullying, family support and feeling safe at school. All scales are standardised within system.

*Scale use.* We build indices of extreme, acquiescent and midpoint responding from 18 questionnaire items unrelated to wellbeing and from the reverse-worded skill items. Students who spent less than one second per questionnaire item are flagged as speeders.

## Groups

We follow the definition of PISA 2025 [@oecd2026vol1]. Disadvantaged and advantaged students are the bottom and top quarters of the status index in their own system, and resilient students are disadvantaged students who score in the top quarter of achievement in their system. Crossing the four quarters of status with the four quarters of reading achievement gives 16 groups (@fig-matrix). We compare four of them: resilient students; disadvantaged low achievers, in the bottom quarter of both; advantaged low achievers; and advantaged top achievers, the reference group in every model. The other 12 groups stay in the models as groups of their own, so that they do not blur the reference. Resilient students make up `r num(100 * mat_rshare(), 1)` per cent of disadvantaged students, close to the OECD figure for reading (13 per cent).

The matrix shows two gradients that run in opposite directions. Life satisfaction rises with status in every quarter of achievement. Among disadvantaged students it falls with achievement, from a mean of `r f2(mat("mean","S1A1"))` in the bottom quarter of achievement to `r f2(mat("mean","S1A4"))` in the top quarter, while among advantaged students it barely varies (`r f2(min(sapply(paste0("S4A", 1:4), function(k) mat("mean", k))))` to `r f2(max(sapply(paste0("S4A", 1:4), function(k) mat("mean", k))))`). Resilient students have the lowest mean of the 16 groups. In every quarter of status the share answering 10 roughly halves from the bottom to the top quarter of achievement, from `r num(100 * mat("ls10","S1A1"), 0)` to `r num(100 * mat("ls10","S1A4"), 0)` per cent among disadvantaged students and from `r num(100 * mat("ls10","S4A1"), 0)` to `r num(100 * mat("ls10","S4A4"), 0)` per cent among advantaged students.

# Empirical approach

## Identification strategy

In each system we estimate, on all students,

$$y_{is} = \alpha_s + \sum_{g \neq g_0} \beta_g D_{gis} + x_{is}'\gamma + \varepsilon_{is},$$

where $y_{is}$ is the standardised life satisfaction of student $i$ in school $s$, $\alpha_s$ is a school fixed effect, $D_{gis}$ equals one if the student belongs to group $g$ of the 16 groups in @fig-matrix, and $x_{is}$ contains the controls. The omitted group $g_0$ is advantaged top achievers, so each $\beta_g$ is the difference in life satisfaction between group $g$ and advantaged top achievers in the same school. The coefficient of resilient students is their gap to advantaged top achievers. Their gaps to advantaged and to disadvantaged low achievers are differences between two coefficients of the same model; the two coefficients share the reference group, and the standard error of the difference accounts for it.

We estimate six nested models on the same students, those observed on every variable the system fielded. Model 1 contains the group indicators only, model 2 adds the school fixed effects, model 3 sex, age and grade, model 4 the six socio-emotional skills, growth mindset, science self-efficacy and enjoyment of science, and model 5 the four relationship scales. Model 6 is model 5 without school fixed effects. A characteristic that a system did not field is left out of that system's models.

We use the final student weights. Standard errors combine the 80 balanced-repeated-replication weights, with Fay's adjustment, and the variation across the ten plausible values. Group membership depends on achievement, so we recompute it for every plausible value and every replicate weight. We pool the system estimates with a random-effects meta-analysis [@dersimonian1986] and report in how many systems an estimate is significant at the 5 per cent level. We call resilient students significantly less satisfied than all three other groups in a system when all three one-sided tests reject at 5 per cent.

*The comparison (RQ1).* The answer to RQ1 is the three contrasts of resilient students in model 3, which compares students in the same school with sex, age and grade held fixed. We also compare resilient students with all other disadvantaged students, using the average of the coefficients of the three lower quarters of achievement, each weighted by its share of those students. To locate the gap on the scale we estimate model 3 for the share of students who give each answer from 0 to 10 and for the share at or above several points of the scale.

*Skills, mindsets and relationships (RQ2).* Models 4 and 5 add the two blocks of characteristics. A decomposition that does not depend on the order in which controls enter attributes the change from model 3 to model 5 to each characteristic [@gelbach2016]: the contribution of a characteristic is the difference between the two groups in that characteristic, from model 3, times its coefficient in model 5.

*Disadvantage among achievers (RQ3).* The difference between the achievement gaps of the two status groups, (resilient students − disadvantaged low achievers) − (advantaged top achievers − advantaged low achievers), comes from the same model. A broader version sets top achievers against all other students of their status group, weighted as above. The cross-section cannot rule out that selection into high achievement differs by family background (see *Selection* below).

*Heterogeneity (RQ4).* Fourteen characteristics may change the gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers, in three groups: the context (the mean status and the mean achievement of schoolmates, each computed without the student, sex, and expecting a university degree), beliefs and attitudes (growth mindset, science self-efficacy, sense of belonging and enjoyment of science) and the six skills. A linear interaction for each characteristic, estimated system by system, imposes a functional form, tests the fourteen separately and without adjustment for one another, and has little power in a single system. We therefore pool the top achievers of the bottom and top status quartiles from all systems, give each system the same total weight, and estimate how the gap varies with all fourteen characteristics at once with a causal forest [@wager2018; @athey2019]. Life satisfaction and the resilient indicator are centred within school, so the gap is identified within schools as in the regressions, and both are first adjusted for the fourteen characteristics, age and grade with regression forests. We report three quantities. A calibration test asks whether the forest finds any variation in the gap beyond its average [@chernozhukov2025]. A projection of the gap on the fourteen characteristics shows which of them carry the variation, each adjusted for the others [@semenova2021]. The gap in each fifth of a characteristic shows the shape without a functional form. Being resilient is not a treatment, and the forest describes how a difference between groups varies. For comparison we report the same forest without school fixed effects, one linear model with school fixed effects and all fourteen interactions on the same pooled sample, and the system-by-system interaction models.

## Methodological threats

*Selection.* The contrasts are conditional differences between groups and have no causal interpretation. Students who reach the top quartile from a poor family may differ from those who do not in temperament, ambition or family circumstances that also shape life satisfaction, and life satisfaction may itself affect effort at school. One design rule follows from the role of skills. Skills help to produce achievement, so a top achiever with few skills must have something unobserved in their favour. We therefore never compare high-skill with low-skill students inside the resilient group. Skills enter as controls or as moderators of the contrast between groups.

*Controls that depend on family background.* Skills, mindsets and relationships are partly shaped by family background and by achievement. Models 4 and 5 therefore do not give a purer estimate of the gap. They show how much of it remains among students with the same characteristics, and the decomposition shows which characteristics account for the difference.

*Schools with both groups.* School fixed effects identify the contrasts from differences within schools. Disadvantaged and advantaged students often attend different schools, so the within-school contrasts rest on socially mixed schools, and they leave out the part of the gap that lies between schools. Model 6 shows the gap without school fixed effects.

*Inference in the forest.* A forest cannot use the replicate weights. Its standard errors are clustered by school, and because group membership depends on the plausible value we grow the forest once for each of the ten plausible values and combine the results in the same way as the regression estimates. The clustered standard errors do not reflect the stratification of the PISA samples.

*Scale use.* All four questions rest on one self-rated item, and students of different ability may answer it differently. In PISA 2018 the answers 0, 5 and 10 become rarer as mathematics scores rise, which @barringtonleigh2024 reads as less numerate students using only the bottom, middle and top of the scale. That explanation cannot produce the gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers, who achieve equally highly. Among Czech fifth-graders, the life-satisfaction advantage of pupils with excellent grades grows after correction with anchoring vignettes [@vonkova2019], which points to a stricter standard among high achievers; a stricter standard among disadvantaged high achievers remains possible. Three checks address it. We add the response-style indices as controls and exclude speeders. We estimate a placebo, the gap in choosing 10 on three effort questions with a 1–10 format. And we fit an ordered-probit model with a separate shift for resilient students at every threshold of the scale.

*Self-rated skills.* A skill rated by the student may moderate the gap because both ratings share reporting habits with life satisfaction. We read the moderation results for self-rated skills with this in mind.

# Results

## Resilient students against the other groups

Resilient students are less satisfied with their lives than all three groups they are compared with (@tbl-models). In the same school and with sex, age and grade held fixed (column 3), they report life satisfaction `r mea("S1A4","M3")` SD below advantaged top achievers (SE `r mse("S1A4","M3")`), or `r mea("S1A4","M3",2,"pt")` points on the 0--10 scale. The gap to advantaged low achievers is almost as large, `r mea("R-AL","M3")` SD (SE `r mse("R-AL","M3")`). Against disadvantaged low achievers it is `r mea("R-PL","M3")` SD (SE `r mse("R-PL","M3")`), and against all other disadvantaged students, the three lower quarters of achievement taken together, `r mea("R-PO","M3")` SD (SE `r mse("R-PO","M3")`). Advantaged students are about equally satisfied whatever their achievement: low achievers among them differ from top achievers by `r me("S4A1","M3")` SD.

The comparisons with advantaged students are the large and consistent ones. The gap to advantaged top achievers is significantly negative in `r msig("S1A4","M3")` of `r mn("S1A4","M3")` systems and the gap to advantaged low achievers in `r msig("R-AL","M3")`, against `r msig("R-PL","M3")` systems for disadvantaged low achievers. Resilient students are significantly less satisfied than all three groups at once in `r mall3("M3")` systems, and in no system and no model are they significantly more satisfied than any of them.

Comparing students within schools makes the gap to advantaged top achievers larger, not smaller. Without controls it is `r mea("S1A4","M1")` SD (column 1). With school fixed effects it is `r mea("S1A4","M2")` SD (column 2), and disadvantaged low achievers move further below the reference group as well, from `r me("S1A1","M1")` to `r me("S1A1","M2")` SD. Disadvantaged students are thus further below advantaged schoolmates than below advantaged students in the system as a whole. Sex, age and grade change little (column 3).

@fig-countries shows the estimates of column 3 for every system. Resilient students are less satisfied than advantaged top achievers in `r mneg("S1A4","M3")` of `r mn("S1A4","M3")` systems and than advantaged low achievers in `r mneg("R-AL","M3")`. The regional means lie between `r num(min(rgp[file == "mxmod" & term == "mm:z:M3:S1A4" & !region %in% c("All systems", "New Zealand and Kenya"), re_mean]))` and `r num(max(rgp[file == "mxmod" & term == "mm:z:M3:S1A4" & !region %in% c("All systems", "New Zealand and Kenya"), re_mean]))` SD against advantaged top achievers and between `r num(min(rgp[file == "mxmod" & term == "mm:z:M3:R-AL" & !region %in% c("All systems", "New Zealand and Kenya"), re_mean]))` and `r num(max(rgp[file == "mxmod" & term == "mm:z:M3:R-AL" & !region %in% c("All systems", "New Zealand and Kenya"), re_mean]))` SD against advantaged low achievers. The gap to advantaged top achievers is largest in Western and Northern Europe and smallest in East and South-East Asia, and the estimate is close to zero in Croatia, Indonesia and the Philippines.

Differences in SD of life satisfaction with 95% intervals. Systems are grouped by region and ranked by their estimate in panel A; New Zealand and Kenya are shown without a region. Filled circles: p < 0.05; filled triangles: p < 0.10; open circles: not significant (two-sided, unadjusted). ## Where on the scale the gap lies

Against advantaged top achievers the whole distribution of answers shifts down (@fig-answers). In model 3, resilient students give the answers 9 and 10 less often, by `r appa("ans:M3:9:R-AT")` and `r appa("ans:M3:10:R-AT")` percentage points, and every answer from 3 to 7 more often, by `r app("ans:M3:4:R-AT")` to `r app("ans:M3:5:R-AT")` points. They are `r appa("thr:M3:ge8:R-AT")` points less likely to answer 8 or more, `r appa("thr:M3:ge6:R-AT")` points less likely to answer 6 or more, and `r app("thr:M3:le3:R-AT")` points more likely to answer 3 or less. Without any adjustment, resilient students answer 10 less often than advantaged top achievers in `r cbelow(mat_sys[CNT %in% MX_SYS], "ls10:S1A4", "ls10:S4A4")` of `r length(MX_SYS)` systems (panel B).

The comparisons with low achievers look different. Against advantaged low achievers and against disadvantaged low achievers the gap lies almost entirely at the top answer: resilient students answer 10 less often by `r appa("ans:M3:10:R-AL")` and `r appa("ans:M3:10:R-PL")` points and answer 7 and 8 more often. Low achievers in both status groups give the top answer far more often than top achievers (@fig-matrix), so what separates resilient students from them is a matter of the highest rating. What separates them from advantaged students of the same achievement is a lower rating across the scale.

![**The gap to advantaged top achievers across the scale.** Panel A: difference between resilient students and advantaged top achievers in the same school in the share giving each answer from 0 to 10, in percentage points, from model 3 of @tbl-models. Thin lines are systems; the black line and squares are the random-effects mean, with its 95% interval shaded. Panel B: unadjusted share of each group answering 10 in each system; under the line of equality resilient students answer 10 less often. The black square marks the mean of systems.](`r fig("fig_p15_answers")`){#fig-answers width=100%}

## What skills, mindsets and relationships account for

Skills, mindsets and relationships account for about half of the gap to advantaged top achievers. Adding the skills, growth mindset, science self-efficacy and enjoyment of science reduces it to `r mea("S1A4","M4")` SD (column 4), and adding the relationship scales to `r mea("S1A4","M5")` SD (SE `r mse("S1A4","M5")`; column 5). The gap shrinks in `r cbelow(mx_sys, "mm:z:M3:S1A4", "mm:z:M5:S1A4")` of `r mn("S1A4","M3")` systems (@fig-controls, panel A). The decomposition of the change from column 3 to column 5 attributes `r gla("R-AT","total")` SD (SE `r glse("R-AT","total")`) to the characteristics, `r gla("R-AT","REL")` SD of it to relationships and `r gla("R-AT","SKMI")` SD to skills and mindsets. Among the relationships, sense of belonging (`r gla("R-AT","BELONG_z")`) and family support (`r gla("R-AT","FAMSUP_z")`) contribute most. Resilient students report a weaker sense of belonging at school and less family support than advantaged students who achieve as highly, and both are associated with higher life satisfaction. @fig-decomposition shows the decomposition system by system (panel A). Where the gap is significant, belonging and family support make up a visible part of it in nearly every system, and part of the gap remains.

The gap to advantaged low achievers has no such explanation. It is `r mea("R-AL","M3")` SD in column 3 and `r mea("R-AL","M5")` SD in column 5, and the characteristics account for `r gl("R-AL","total")` SD of it (SE `r glse("R-AL","total")`), because resilient students and advantaged low achievers differ little in them (@fig-decomposition, panel B).

Against other disadvantaged students the same characteristics work in the opposite direction. Resilient students have more family support, a stronger sense of belonging and more perseverance than disadvantaged low achievers, so holding these fixed widens the gap from `r mea("R-PL","M3")` to `r mea("R-PL","M5")` SD; they hide `r gl("R-PL","total")` SD of it. Against all other disadvantaged students the gap widens from `r mea("R-PO","M3")` to `r mea("R-PO","M5")` SD. A comparison within the disadvantaged group therefore understates how much less satisfied resilient students are than their characteristics would predict.

Without school fixed effects but with every characteristic held fixed (column 6), the gap to advantaged top achievers is `r mea("S1A4","M6")` SD. Part of what remains within schools reflects how disadvantaged and advantaged students are distributed across schools.

The gap is close to the same in every system. Panel B of @fig-controls plots each system's gap in model 3 against its standard error. If every system had the pooled gap, 95 per cent of the estimates would fall inside the funnel, and about `r round(0.05 * mn("S1A4","M3"))` of `r mn("S1A4","M3")` would fall outside by chance. Of the `r mn("S1A4","M3")` systems, `r mfun("S1A4","M3")` fall inside; the four outside are `r mfun_out("S1A4","M3")`. The share of the variation between systems that sampling error does not explain is `r mI2("S1A4","M3")` per cent, and the between-system standard deviation is `r mtau("S1A4","M3")` SD, small beside a gap of `r mea("S1A4","M3")` SD. With the characteristics held fixed the between-system variance is estimated at zero (I² = `r mI2("S1A4","M5")` per cent), and so it is for the gap to advantaged low achievers in every model. A system in which the gap is not significant is therefore not a system without a gap. Single systems are estimated with standard errors of `r mse_range("S1A4","M3")` SD, and most of these systems lie inside the funnel. The funnel serves here only to judge how far systems differ; every participating system is reported, so it carries no information about selective publication.

![**Characteristics account for part of the gap to advantaged top achievers, and the gap is similar across systems.** Panel A: each system's gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers in model 3 (sex, age and grade held fixed) against the gap in model 5 (skills, mindsets and relationships also held fixed); under the line of equality the gap is larger before the characteristics are held fixed. Panel B: the model-3 gap against its standard error, on a log scale, most precise at the top; the funnel is the region in which 95% of the estimates would fall if every system had the pooled gap (vertical line). Labels are PISA system codes. The black square marks the random-effects mean of systems.](`r fig("fig_p13_controls")`){#fig-controls width=100%}

![**What accounts for the gap, system by system.** Gelbach decomposition of each system's model-3 gap (marker) into the contributions of the characteristics added in models 4 and 5, each the difference between the two groups in the characteristic times its coefficient in model 5, and the remainder, the gap left in model 5. The parts sum to the gap. Panel A: resilient students against advantaged top achievers. Panel B: resilient students against advantaged low achievers. Markers give the significance of the model-3 gap: filled circle p < 0.05, filled triangle p < 0.10, open circle not significant; bars of systems with a non-significant gap are drawn in pale colours. A characteristic a system did not field contributes nothing there. Last row: mean of systems.](`r fig("fig_p14_decomposition")`){#fig-decomposition width=100%}

## Whether the cost is specific to disadvantaged students

High achievers report lower life satisfaction among advantaged students as well, once their characteristics are held fixed: advantaged top achievers are `r num(abs(mrow(mxt("S4A1","M5"))$re_mean))` SD less satisfied than advantaged low achievers in column 5. The difference between top and low achievers is larger among disadvantaged students. Comparing the bottom with the top quarter of achievement, it is larger by `r mea("DiD","M1")` SD without controls (SE `r mse("DiD","M1")`), `r mea("DiD","M3")` SD in column 3 and `r mea("DiD","M5")` SD in column 5 (SE `r mse("DiD","M5")`). Comparing top achievers with all other students of the same status group gives `r mea("DiD2","M1")`, `r mea("DiD2","M3")` and `r mea("DiD2","M5")` SD (SE about `r mse("DiD2","M3",3)`), the same in every model. These differences are significant in the pooled estimates and in at most `r max(sapply(paste0("M", 1:6), function(m) msig("DiD2", m)))` single systems. The lower life satisfaction of high achievers is general, and it is somewhat larger among disadvantaged students.

## Where the gap differs

Within schools the causal forest finds no variation in the gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers. The calibration coefficient for variation is `r f_("calib","differential")` (SE `r fse("calib","differential")`), where a forest whose predictions track real differences would give a value near one, and none of the fourteen characteristics has a significant coefficient in the projection of the gap on all of them (@fig-forest). The forest's average gap is `r fes("ate","gap")`. It adjusts for all fourteen characteristics and is less precise than the regressions: in a typical plausible value only `r big(mean(finfo$n_sch_both))` of `r big(mean(finfo$n_sch))` schools contain both groups. Without school fixed effects the forest does not find variation either (calibration coefficient `r f_("calib","differential", model_ = "nofe")`, SE `r fse("calib","differential", model_ = "nofe")`).

![**The gap at each level of fourteen characteristics.** Causal-forest estimates of the within-school gap between resilient students and advantaged top achievers in each fifth of a continuous characteristic, or in each category of an indicator, pooled over all systems, with 95% intervals. The dotted line is the forest's average gap. Schoolmates' status and achievement are computed without the student.](`r fig("fig_p5_forest")`){#fig-forest width=100%}

The linear models point to one characteristic. In a within-school model with all fourteen interactions on the pooled sample, each SD of sense of belonging makes the gap smaller by `r fes("ols","BELONG")`. In the system-by-system interaction models (@fig-interactions in the appendix) the same holds, `r esp("mech","mod:BELONG:topX")`, and belonging is the only characteristic that passes a Bonferroni threshold for fourteen tests. Self-regulated learning (`r esp("mech","mod:SELFREG:topX")`) and expecting a university degree (`r esp("mech","mod:uni:topX")`, a larger gap) are significant at 5 per cent without the correction. Schoolmates' status and achievement, sex and growth mindset do not change the gap.

## Robustness

The gap does not come from how resilient students use response scales. They are less extreme responders than advantaged top achievers on items unrelated to wellbeing (`r ae("rsgap:ERS_z:R-AT")` SD), and holding four response-style indices fixed changes the model-3 gap from `r ae("rs:M3:R-AT")` to `r ae("rs:M3rs:R-AT")` SD on the same students. Excluding students who answered the questionnaire very fast leaves it at `r ae("rs:M3nospeed:R-AT")` SD. On three effort questions with a 1--10 format, resilient students choose 10 about as often as advantaged top achievers (differences of `r app("plac:EFF1_10:R-AT")`, `r app("plac:EFF2_10:R-AT")` and `r app("plac:EFFQ_10:R-AT")` points), and the shortfall of 10s on life satisfaction is `r appa("plac:LS10:R-AT")` points before and `r appa("plac:LS10net:R-AT")` points after those answers are held fixed.

An ordered-probit model with a separate shift for resilient students at every threshold of the scale shows the shift across the scale that @fig-answers suggests. With sex, age and grade held fixed, the latent shift is between `r num(min(abs(thrm[term %in% paste0("gop:demo:b", 4:8), est])))` and `r num(max(abs(thrm[term %in% paste0("gop:demo:b", 4:8), est])))` SD at the thresholds from 4 to 8 and `r tm("gop:demo:b10", mag = TRUE)` SD at 10; a single shift gives `r tm("op:demo:top", mag = TRUE)` SD. The gap is not confined to the top answer, which a stricter standard for a 10 alone would produce. With the response-style indices also allowed to move every threshold, the shift at 10 is `r tm("hop:sei:b10", mag = TRUE)` SD.

Coarser use of the scale by less numerate students, who answer 0, 5 and 10 more often [@barringtonleigh2024], cannot produce a gap between groups that achieve equally highly, and resilient students give the answer 5 more often than advantaged top achievers, not less.

With achievement measured by science, in `r mscn("S1A4","M3")` systems, the gap to advantaged top achievers is `r msc("S1A4","M3")` SD in model 3 and `r msc("S1A4","M5")` SD in model 5, the gap to advantaged low achievers `r msc("R-AL","M3")` SD, and the difference between the achievement gaps of the two status groups `r msc("DiD2","M3")` SD. Against advantaged top achievers resilient students answer 9 and 10 less often by `r appa("ans:M3:9:R-AT", tab = mxas)` and `r appa("ans:M3:10:R-AT", tab = mxas)` points.

# Discussion

## Findings and interpretation

Resilient students are less satisfied with their lives than advantaged students of the same achievement, than advantaged students who achieve much less, and than disadvantaged students who achieve much less. The first two gaps are large and similar across education systems. The third is small. This ordering explains why the evidence so far has looked mixed. The OECD compared resilient students with all other disadvantaged students at a cut point of 7 and found small differences of both signs [@oecd2019]. In our data the comparison with all other disadvantaged students gives `r mea("R-PO","M3")` SD and is significant in `r msig("R-PO","M3")` systems, close to that picture. Against advantaged students the gap is four to five times as large.

Within the disadvantaged group the gap is small because resilient students bring more of what is associated with life satisfaction: more family support, a stronger sense of belonging and more perseverance. With these held fixed it more than doubles. Against advantaged students who achieve as highly the balance runs the other way. Resilient students report less family support and a weaker sense of belonging, and these two characteristics account for close to a third of the gap. A high achiever from a poor family thus has fewer of the relationships associated with life satisfaction than a high achiever from a rich family, and more of them than a poor low achiever. Family support is the strongest correlate of adolescents' life satisfaction across countries [@bi2021], and belonging is a consistent one in PISA [@oecd2019b]. The gap to advantaged low achievers has no such account: the two groups differ little in these characteristics, and resilient students remain `r mea("R-AL","M5")` SD behind with all of them held fixed.

The shape of the gap differs by comparison. Against low achievers in either status group, resilient students mainly give fewer answers of 10, the pattern of the inverted-U relation between achievement and life satisfaction [@oecd2019b; @li2024]. Against advantaged top achievers the distribution shifts down across the scale, with fewer high answers and more middle and low ones. A stricter standard for the top answer would produce the first pattern. It cannot produce the second, and the threshold model shows a shift of similar size at every threshold up to 9, and a smaller one at 10. The comparison with advantaged top achievers is therefore the one least likely to reflect reporting.

The results bear on the studies of skin-deep resilience, which find that disadvantaged young people who succeed have fewer depressive symptoms than their disadvantaged peers [@brody2013; @miller2015]. Our comparison within the disadvantaged group is consistent with that: resilient students are no more likely than disadvantaged low achievers to give a low answer. Against advantaged peers they are more likely to give one. Success from a poor background may protect against distress relative to other poor young people and still leave a shortfall relative to those who succeed from a better start.

Lower life satisfaction among high achievers is not specific to the poor. Advantaged top achievers report less than advantaged low achievers once their characteristics are held fixed. The difference is larger among disadvantaged students, by about `r mea("DiD2","M3")` SD in every model, a modest addition to a general pattern.

Context does not change the gap. The causal forest finds no variation within schools, and neither the status nor the achievement of schoolmates moderates the gap in linear models, against the two mechanisms with the clearest support in earlier work, comparison with higher-achieving classmates [@rathmann2018] and the position of a poor student among better-off schoolmates [@crosnoe2009]. The one consistent moderator is sense of belonging, the same characteristic that accounts for much of the gap. Resilient students who feel they belong at school are closer to advantaged top achievers. Both results rest on self-report and on a cross-section.

## Implications for indicators of resilience

Academic resilience is reported as a success of education systems. It should be reported with what resilient students say about their lives, and with a comparison that includes advantaged students. A comparison within the disadvantaged group, the one used so far, shows the smallest gap and is offset by the relationships that resilient students have. An indicator defined as the share of students above a cut point can also miss part of the difference: against disadvantaged low achievers it lies almost entirely at the top answer and barely shows at the usual cut point of 7. School belonging is the characteristic most closely tied to the gap, both as part of it and as a moderator, and it can be measured in every PISA cycle.

## Limitations

These conclusions have limits. The data are a cross-section, and the comparisons are differences between groups that may differ in unobserved ways. Skills, mindsets and relationships are partly shaped by family background and achievement, so the decomposition describes the gap and does not separate causes. The outcome is a single item. The models use students observed on every characteristic, and low achievers are more often missing one, which may make the low-achieving groups look slightly different from all low achievers. PISA 2025 measures task-oriented skills, so we cannot say whether optimism or emotional regulation would account for more of the gap. The forest has limited power, because fewer than half of the schools contain both resilient students and advantaged top achievers. And the research questions were formulated while we explored these data, so the results await replication.

# Conclusion

Across `r N_mx$systems` education systems, students from the poorest quarter of families who reach the top quarter of reading achievement rate their lives lower than students from the richest quarter, whether those students achieve as much or much less. The distance to advantaged students of the same achievement is `r mea("S1A4","M3")` SD, about `r mea("S1A4","M3",1,"pt")` points on the 0--10 scale, and it covers the whole scale rather than only the top answer. About a third of it is associated with weaker belonging at school and less family support. Measured against other disadvantaged students, the usual comparison, the gap is small, because resilient students have more of these relationships than poor students who achieve less.

Systems that count resilient students as a success have reason to ask those students how their lives are going and to compare their answers with those of advantaged students. The finding gives no argument for expecting less of disadvantaged students, and it does not establish that achievement harms them.

Two additions to the data would decide between the readings that remain open. A panel that follows students through school would show whether weaker relationships come before the gap or after it. A PISA cycle with anchoring vignettes for life satisfaction, or with a second wellbeing measure, would separate a stricter standard for a good life from lower satisfaction with it.
